line: Yeah, holy matrimony where I stack the cake up

meaning:
In the line “holy matrimony where I stack the cake up,” Big Sean is playing with the double meaning of the words “holy matrimony” and “cake.”

Holy Matrimony: Traditionally, this phrase refers to marriage, often seen as a sacred or religious union.
Cake: In slang, “cake” can refer to money, so “stacking the cake” means accumulating wealth.

By combining these ideas, Big Sean is saying that his relationship with money is like a marriage – serious, committed, and fruitful. “Stack the cake up” suggests that he’s building his wealth consistently, just like how one might build a successful marriage. It’s a clever way to emphasize his focus on securing financial success, treating it with the same seriousness as one would treat a marriage.

meaning:
Big Sean reps for the Detroit Red Wings—an ice hockey team based in his hometown. In 1994, journalists captured an image of 2Pac leaving court in a Red Wings jersey, which has turned into a symbol of Detroit pride. In addition, Sean seems to be twisting a few lines from 2Pac’s October 1993 single, “Keep Ya Head Up”:

Some say the blacker the berry, the sweeter the juice
I say the darker the flesh, then the deeper the roots



From left to right: Big Sean, 2Pac, and The Spirit of Detroit in Red Wings jerseys.

The phrase “the blacker the berry” stems from Wallace Thurman’s 1929 novel of the same name. Sean uses the line to address racism—in  June 2020, protests were ignited by the killings of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and Ahmaud Arbery. Sean joined protesters in Los Angeles and opened up about partaking in protests on social media:

I don’t know if it’s to make us look like we wild beasts or don’t have control, but we clearly are not wild beasts. We’re extraordinary, talented magical people that if you took us out of the equation, the world would be very, very bland.

It’s also worth noting that Sean uses some clever wordplay by spelling out his rap name, “Big” Sean, to compare himself to The Notorious B.I.G., who feuded with 2Pac in 1995–1996. This is not the first time that Sean spells out his name—on YG’s 2018 track, “BIG BANK,” he says:

I said, ‘Bitch, I'ma do me’
B.I.G., bitch everything zoomed-in (zoom)

It’s a clever wordplay that distinguishes him from others who use the term “dope” for illicit activities.

line: Torn achilles limpin’ to the free throw line, yeah
vault_lines: Torn achilles limpin' to the free throw line, yeah
meaning:
On April 12, 2013 Kobe Bryant tore his achilles tendon after an innocent push off his left foot. After this injury however, Bryant decided to get back up, and he limped to the free throw line and made both shots, which instantly exuded a round of applause from fans and teammates alike. Speaking on his injury in the locker room that night, Kobe explained:

When I first did it, right there, I was trying to feel if the tendon is there or if it’s gone. I realized it wasn’t there. I was literally trying to pull the tendon up, so hopefully I could walk and kind of hobble through the last two and a half minutes and try to play.

This is a prime example of Kobe’s famous mindset, the Mamba Mentality, as it simply means putting in the determination and work to be better every single day.

line: Fuck twenty-four Seven, I’m goin’ twenty-four eight Fuck twenty-four Seven, I’m goin’ twenty-four eight That’s Magic, and he know what it took to be great
vault_lines: Fuck twenty-four Seven, I'm goin' twenty-four eight
meaning:
24/7 is shorthand for 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. It is commonly used when people refer to something that is being done all the time.

24 and 8 are the two numbers Kobe Bryant wore during his time with the Los Angeles Lakers. Kobe started his career with the number 8, which pays homage to the number he wore while he played in Italy and the sum of the numbers he wore during an Adidas ABCD youth training camp (Kobe wore number 143). At the start of the 2006-2007 season, Kobe changed to number 24, which is the number he wore during his high school career. Both numbers would be retired by the Los Angeles Lakers in 2017.



The sum of 24 and 8 add up to 32, which is the number Magic Johnson, another former player for the Los Angeles Lakers, wore during his tenure. Johnson’s number was retired by the Lakers in 1992. Magic Johnson had a very successful career, becoming a 5-time NBA champion and 12-time NBA All-Star, amongst many other achievements.

Beyoncé’s vocals turn this verse into a bold, commanding moment. The first line—“When it’s time to go, where you tryna go?”—reads as a confident challenge, asserting presence and control over the situation. Delivered by Beyoncé, it carries a sense of empowerment and authority, emphasizing her role as someone whose influence can’t be ignored.

Beyoncé’s performance underscores the demand for acknowledgment, reflecting the larger theme of the song: being seen, celebrated, and respected for success. line: Somebody need to put us on camera The world of Rollies and everyone families
vault_lines: Somebody need to put us on camera
meaning:
These lines emphasize Kanye’s fascination with fame, luxury, and visibility. “Somebody need to put us on camera” suggests a desire to be documented—either literally for media attention or metaphorically as a way of immortalizing the lifestyle he and his circle are living. It reflects the performative nature of celebrity, where every action is on display.

The second line—“The world of Rollies and everyone families”—highlights the opulence of Kanye’s life, referencing Rolex watches as a symbol of wealth and status. It also hints at legacy and connections, showing that in this world, relationships (both familial and social) are intertwined with material success.

Together, the lines underscore a recurring theme in Kanye’s work: the intersection of luxury, fame, and the way public scrutiny shapes personal life.

line: No women in the crowd, screamin’ and it’s loud Doin’ things not allowed and I swear it’s going down right now
vault_lines: No women in the crowd, screamin' and it's loud

These lines depict a raw, high-energy scene, likely at a party or club, emphasizing chaos and rebellion. The first line—“No women in the crowd, screamin’ and it’s loud”—sets the scene of an all-male, hype-driven environment, suggesting exclusivity and the intensity of male camaraderie.

The second line—“Doin’ things not allowed and I swear it’s going down right now”—reflects the thrill of breaking rules, living in the moment, and indulging in behavior that society might deem inappropriate. It underscores Kanye’s recurring theme of indulgence, recklessness, and the consequences of fame and youth.

Overall, this verse captures the feeling of uncontrolled energy and immediate gratification, common in Kanye’s more braggadocious and street-oriented tracks.

These lines highlight the transactional and performative nature of fame, money, and relationships in Kanye’s world. The first line, “Get what you ask for, I swear that your ass slow,” can be seen as a commentary on people who struggle to match ambition with action—basically, asking for success but moving too slowly to achieve it.

The next line references physical attraction and sexualized expectations—“She got a big booty but she couldn’t drop it as low”—which plays into the hip-hop trope of admiring physical appearance while also critiquing performative behaviors in relationships.

“'Til you take your last ho and rope up all the cashflow” suggests that people only pay attention when someone reaches financial success, a recurring theme in Kanye’s work: wealth dictates attention and loyalty. The final line, “When you gettin' money they be all up on your ass, yo,” drives this home: fame and money bring opportunistic relationships and shallow interest.

Overall, this verse blends humor, critique of materialism, and Kanye’s candid observations on social dynamics around wealth and fame.

line: These bars could put bad boys on death row Kinda crazy how Suge and Puff in jail, though (Damn) (Woah) Yo, I was at the party but I never seen a freak-off (Woah) Instead, a battle rapper on stage showing his cheeks off (Ayo) (Yeah)
vault_lines: These bars could put bad boys on death row
meaning:
These bars open with Joey referencing Bad Boy Entertainment and Death Row Records, two famous record labels in the 1990s that were owned by Diddy and Suge Knight respectively.

In 2018, Suge was sentenced to 28 years in prison due to a fatal hit-and-run incident in 2015. He will not be eligible for parole until 2034. Meanwhile, in 2024, Diddy was arrested and indicted in New York for racketeering, sex trafficking by force, and transportation for purposes of prostitution. As of this song’s release, Diddy is currently on trial for these charges.

Before his arrest, many of Diddy’s sex crimes allegedly occurred during his parties, or “freak-offs”. Several alleged victims described the things that Diddy did during these “freak-offs”, such as drugging and raping women. Joey admits that he has attended Diddy’s parties before, but he has never once attended a “freak-off”. Joey and Diddy also collaborated on the song “The Baddest” from Joey’s 2022 album, 2000.



The battle rapper showing his cheeks in question is likely Daylyt. While a formidable lyricist, Daylyt has a history of performing outrageous antics for the sake of his battles, even infamously defecating on stage in 2014. Joey addresses Daylyt in a more direct manner later on in this verse.

line: B-I-G minus the East and West beef
vault_lines: B-I-G minus the East and West beef
meaning:
Big Sean commonly refers to himself as “B-I-G Sean”, a subtle nod to deceased rapper The Notorious B.I.G.. In the mid-1990s, Biggie was embroiled in the East Coast and West Coast rivalry, which ultimately led to his and 2Pac’s deaths in 1997.

The line also alludes to Joey Bada$$ and Ab-Soul’s appearances on the song. Earlier in 2025, Joey released the song “The Ruler’s Back”, which attempted to start another East Coast and West Coast beef. This makes Ab-Soul’s appearance here especially interesting since he is from the West Coast.

“When I die, on my tombstone, it’s gonna say: ‘I deserved to be here because I signed Big Sean.’”

A month later, Big Sean responded to Ye’s comments during his own interview on Drink Champs, calling it “some bitch-ass shit.”

In 2024, Big Sean took another subliminal shot at Ye in his “On The Radar Freestyle,” rapping:

I seen grown men get matching tattoos for the clout

Ab-Soul’s adlib, “Yea or nay?,” makes it even clearer that this is a shot at Kanye via the homophonic reference to his current name, Ye.

line: In which case Joey, you put me in a sticky predicament (I did) I had to show solidarity to my syndicate (Come on, Soul) Nah, you know anybody can get it In such a way that it will make any physician conflicted But listen, the 47's still on my tricep (Facts) Pass the pot, let me skill it, I’m quite the chef Pro Era the masters, that ain’t ever incorrect (That’s right) But it’s still TDE till 3000 and forever Lyt was heavy and Ray definitely stepped But this is hip-hop, you know we still on that It was healthy for the sport, stickin’ to the roots, keepin’ it competitive Just be lucky that Soul ain’t steppin’ in (Hahahaha) All of y’all would’ve had to shoot (Yeah) (F’real)
vault_lines: Now how can I say this all in a nice way?
meaning:
Joey Bada$$ kicked off 2025 in explosive fashion with the release of his single, “The Ruler’s Back”, in which he dissed Kendrick Lamar and tried to ignite a beef between the East Coast and West Coast. In response, West Coast rappers Daylyt and Ray Vaughn released diss tracks aimed at Joey.

This left Ab-Soul conflicted because he clearly has tons of respect for Joey; however, he is also friends with Daylyt and Ray and feels that he must represent for his peers in the West Coast.

To appease both sides, Ab-Soul starts by mentioning the 47 tattoos on his triceps, which was done in memory of Joey’s friend, Capital STEEZ, who died in 2012. It’s worthy to note that Ab-Soul released a song titled “47 Bars” in honor of Capital STEEZ in 2015.



The 47 symbol was the old logo of hip-hop collective, Pro Era, which both Joey and STEEZ were apart of. Afterward, he honors STEEZ again by referencing a line from his 2012 song, “Chicago”:

Keep a stash, even when my pockets was lookin' thin
So pass the pot and let me skillet

Ab-Soul salutes Pro Era, and recognizes that Joey said what he said because hip-hop is a competitive sport. He then directly Lyt and Ray in what can be interpreted as a double entendre. In the line, “Lyt was heavy” Ab-Soul is not only referring to the rapper, Daylyt, but also the word “light”, referring to something that doesn’t have much weight. He continues the wordplay on weight by describing Daylyt’s disses as “heavy”, or very intense. Ab-Soul uses juxtaposition to show appreciate to Daylyt.

At the end, though, Ab-Soul assures that he will always represent for his label, Top Dawg Entertainment, and warns that he will destroy any rapper who tries a rap beef with him.

line: Roc-A-Fella chain, but you can still get Ether’d

meaning:
This is a reference to Nas' 2001 diss track “Ether,” which was aimed at JAY-Z, the head of Roc-A-Fella Records. The song is regarded as one of the best disses in rap history, and caused the term “ether” to become synonymous with roasting someone to the point of humiliation. Sean’s warning his competition (potentially Kendrick Lamar in particular) that he won’t hesitate to put them on blast in the same way.

In February 2017, JAY-Z presented Big Sean with a coveted Roc-A-Fella chain following the release of his album I Decided.  The chain is usually given to those who sign to Roc Nation, but JAY has made it a custom to present the chain to artists he feels have properly established themselves in the rap game.

Sean has used his imagery before in his feature on the 2016 G.O.O.D Music collab “Champions”:

Another common motif of rap is the idea of a smaller crew and caring for your family. Consequentially, the idea of “fakes” trying to swindle you has also become widespread, as in YG’s 2016 song “Gimmie Got Shot”:

vault_lines: I'm about rollin' a seven when I toss up the dice (Dice)
meaning:
Craps is a dice game where players wager money on the outcome of dice rolls.

“Pass line” is the basic bet in the game, which is a bet for the shooter to win.

Seven is a natural number in craps, which means everyone who bets the pass line gets paid when the shooter rolls a seven. If the shooter were to always roll a seven, they would always win.

If someone jacks (or bites) Eminem’s style, he’ll “grade” (or “grate” like a cheese grater) you like a math paper, making sure he’s the last face you see before you die—a clever double entendre with the meanings of “pass”.

line: [Intro: Fuzzy Jones]
vault_lines: Well, it is a weepin' and a moanin' and a gnashin' of teeth
meaning:
As revealed in an interview with Hip-Hop Wired, Chicago legend The Twilight Tone dug up this sample of Fuzzy Jones, a legend in dancehall for his work on dubplates and in sound clashing culture.


Then we just got to talking and I just thought, ‘What could I do that would just be counter establishment? Or counter cliché, like what could I put on there.?‘ For some reason, I heard that dude [in the beginning of the track], I heard him, I had a vision. I heard that  ‘Well it’s the weeping and the moaning’ and I was like ‘Oh!‘ Then it just literally, I hate to sound so like comic book or some sh-t, but literally I was like ‘Oh my God,’ like I had chills. So then, I was invited to the studio. I talked him, maybe that was Friday, or Saturday, We met up.

“The next day he invited me to the studio, and he was there and a couple of his crew, and I played the sample and everybody froze, everybody paused. Like everybody. It’s just that everybody was keyed to it. and Ye was like ‘Oh snap,‘ and he started hitting the buttons on it. The rest is, as you would say, history or our story.”


This particular intro comes from Dust A Soundboy by Super Beagle, released originally in 1996. It came out on Technique Record’s version of the Stalag 17 Riddim, which was originally produced in 1973 by Winston Riley and has heralded over 300 songs.

In this case, Kanye’s rivals will be tearing their hair out and cursing themselves for not being able to compete with G.O.O.D. Music, Hip-Hop’s champion sound.

The good folks over at Large Up did a great write up on the Dust a Sound Boy that you can read here, and also put up one of the few photos on Mr. Jones.

With songs like “Paranoid” (808s) and even back to “The New Workout Plan” as evidence, we know Kanye’s not really that uncomfortable fucking with Electro-house, 80s House, and Indie–all in a Hip-Hop song. The intro is performed by actor J.R. Starr, known for his performance in films like The Great Venice Robbery and Lust for Love.

At the end of the intro, Sean’s older self gets hit by a car and is reincarnated as his present day self. This is why song two is titled “Light”—it represents walking into the light after you die.

Sean explained the concept of the album on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon:

The concept of the album is this is me & this is an older version of me. It’s parallel right there with each other, but the name of the album is ‘I Decided.’ I realized my whole life changed when I decided. I feel like life is about making right decisions at any point, or the wrong decisions. So the album is basically like having that wisdom of an old man while you’re young and going through life & figuring it out.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V22HHCkPneI

I was at McDonald’s, paying with change out of my pocket. There was times where I was spending my last $40 on studio sessions, times where my parents didn’t have money for clothes, new this and new that. I had to go out and figure that out on my own.

line: You got me hypnotized like the scene with Big and I, reverse wheelin’ (Damn)
vault_lines: You got me hypnotized like the scene with Big and I, reverse wheelin' (Damn)

Biggie, Biggie, Biggie, can’t you see?
Sometimes your words just hypnotize me

Diddy is specifically alluding to the car chase scene in the music video of “Hypnotize,” where the two rappers attempt to escape the police by driving their convertible in reverse.



“Reverse wheelin'” could also be a slight callback to Biggie’s unsolved  drive-by murder, which occurred on March 9, 1997, a week after “Hypnotize” was released. Diddy and Biggie were travelling together in two separate vehicles—Biggie’s vehicle was ambushed at the red light moments after Diddy’s leading vehicle blew through the yellow light.

Diddy has admitted that he feels responsible for Biggie’s death in an interview on The Wendy Williams Show on June 29, 2017:

I think I’ll always feel some sort of responsibility because I’m in this thing with him. […] That’s something that really bothered me throughout my life.

On March 9, 2020, the 23rd anniversary of Biggie’s passing, Diddy shared a “Hypnotize” anecdote in an Instagram post:

This candid moment when BIG was having writer’s block. This only happened to him once. He was talking about retiring. And I’m basically just telling him to stop talking crazy and that he was the greatest of all time. Then he went in and made hypnotize!

line: Welcome to the terrordome

meaning:
“Welcome to the Terrordome” is a January 1990 single from rap group Public Enemy. The phrase, first coined by the group in the title of the aforementioned song, has gone on to be interpolated in many modern rap songs, such as Pusha T’s “Trouble on My Mind.”

The phrase is very racially-charged and was even back when it was made. When the song was released and he was asked about the title in an interview with Spin Magazine, Chuck D, a member of Public Enemy, said:

‘Welcome to the Terrordome,‘ what does it mean? It means the 1990’s are coming, if we as a people do the right thing we’ll be all right, if we do the wrong thing the black situation is out of here at the end of the decade. The terrordome is the 1990’s. I got it from this article called “Welcome to the Terrordome’ that was in Melody Maker magazine. I just changed it to Terrordome, the house of the 90’s.

Sean uses the phrase in reference to his childhood in his hometown Detroit. Speaking in the same frame of reference of his childhood traits and desires, Sean calls his hometown his “terrordome” that he has to get out of and advance from as a black male.

line: So when I’m rippin’, it’s hard to tell whether if it is really because Of how offensive I am, or just what a bitch that you are Like I never had to get my clothes at fucking St. Vincent de Paul Like I don’t make sure every sentence and bar with a pencil is sharp, and I’m quick on the draw
vault_lines: I'm the originator, make it, then I make more
meaning:
Em questions the motives behind public backlash he has continued to receive for controversial lyrics often aimed at other celebrities. To do so, he employs “rip” as a double entendre to mean harsh criticism and a physical tear.

Following the release of his album, Music to Be Murdered By in January of 2020, Em received condemnation from some for his discussion of the 2017 Las Vegas mass shooting and Manchester Arena bombing, among other topics. Here, he asks whether those who are upset at him are truly upset or simply too sensitive.

Defending his reputation, Em asserts that disapproval of his “ripping” has not held him back, despite attempts to leave him with tattered clothes or a torn paper for his raps. Growing up in Detroit, he reflects that he previously sought help from St. Vincent de Paul, an American emergency resource organization which provides  food and clothing to those in need. For his tracks, Em ensures he is always quick-witted and severe with his word-play. Here, “sharp” and “quick on the draw” take on multiple meanings, referring to both a pencil and a possibly deadly response. Em’s words are his weapon.

Big Sean uses these two lines to, once again, illustrate the lavish lifestyle he wishes his work as a rapper will help him achieve. In order to do so, Sean uses the popular ‘noun on noun’ ebonic structure (ie. ‘girls on girls’ and ‘pools on pools’) which is meant to show material excess. By using the ‘noun on noun’ structure, Sean is implying that he has so many bills, pools and girls that they have to be stacked onto one another. A style best popularized by YC in his song ‘Stacks’: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r5w21_Vphbg

Big Sean also references Moulin Rouge, the famous cabaret in Paris (a popular vacation destination for the members of G.O.O.D. Music). https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c59ifR0PEkY
Moulin Rouge, the birthplace of the seductive can-can dance, is used here to indicate that his aforementioned ‘girls on girls’ are wearing lingerie and dancing sexually and seductively for him.



This line may also refer to Baz Luhrman’s 2001 movie ‘Moulin Rouge’ in which a poet (in this case, Big Sean) falls for a beautiful courtesan (also in this case, Big Sean’s singing and dancing girlfriend Naya Riviera).

line: In a lofty place tanglin’ with Satan over history

meaning:
Jay’s struggle isn’t that much different than any of ours. In “tangling with Satan,” Jay is fighting evil forces, both external and internal, for the fate of his own soul.

In the Bible, it was the triumph of God’s army of angels over Lucifer and his demons that determined the course of human history by allowing us to live free of evil, granting us the free will to make our own decisions.

Through his faith, Jay Electronica has chosen to continue battling these evils on the path toward righteousness. The “lofty place” he’s referring to could be his heightened spiritual state of consciousness or Heaven itself, if he is in fact channeling the perspective of a god in this verse.



In typical Jay Elec fashion, though, there is multiplicity here. Being in a relationship with heiress Kate Rothschild has landed him in the mix with people of a higher socioeconomic status than him (“lofty places”). These people, most likely being older, White men, have a drastically different outlook on life, politics, and religion than he does, and he must engage (“tangle”) with them.



Jay, being a known disciple of the Nation of Islam, could be referring to these powerful white men and the oppressive sociopolitical forces that they represent as “Satan,” or the equivalent of “The Man,” as many Black Muslims have been known to do in the past.
The Nation of Islam holds the belief that Blacks in America are the descendants of great African kingdoms and that, in being taken from their homeland and stripped of their native culture, Blacks were denied their history and have continued to be by the American educational system, which has a reputation for glossing over Black history.
For Jay to “tangle with Satan over history,” then, is for him to argue with these men over the legitimacy of the history they’ve been fed, since, after all, history belongs to the victors.

Members of the organization call themselves Allah’s Five Percenters, which reflects the concept that ten percent of the people of the world know the truth of existence, and those elites [in this case, powerful white men] opt to keep eighty-five percent of the world in ignorance and under their controlling thumb. The five percent are those who know the truth and are determined to enlighten the rest.

Note: The invocation of the Muslim religion here connects very nicely to the Islamic phrase in the next line.

Jay could mean that this verse he is about to deliver is classic in the same way that so many EWF records have become classic. Jay could also mean that he rocked the verse (“earth”), blew it away (“wind”), and spit “fire” – all meaning that he performed incredibly well.

The “rain”/“reign” homophone further suggests Jay’s lyrical dominance. Furthermore, mentioning “rain” strings together water as the fourth element along with earth, wind, and fire. By saying he brings all of these together on a song, Jay is saying that, as a rapper, he can do it all.

The early allusion to the worldly elements set up some of the nature imagery he establishes later, with his following references to nooks, rocks, flowers, rain, and light and darkness.



In a subtle way, Jay showcases his mastery of rap by telling us from the outset the kind of language and imagery he is about to use and remaining consistent throughout the verse while adding new layers of meaning to it (although this song has no hook, but we’ll give Jay Elec a pass on that one).

The Magnolia Projects in New Orleans is one of the most dangerous areas in all of America. These rough streets have been called-out by Jay before, and he’s not the only rapper to have love and admiration for the projects, as well as claims of grandeur inside of them. Despite these extremely rough and impoverished upbringings, Jay has made it out a king among men.



Take care to note this line juxtaposes two possible images presented before you. Without the context of Jay’s history, he paints the beginning of a folkloric tale, where a wild flower(Magnolia) births a “magnificent king” and soldiers.

On the other hand, with Jay’s history, the picture becomes a grungier, darker one. A picture where young men and women starve, get shot, and literally have to fight for their lives. Where these same young men become soldiers, Jay became a king. Also, notice the subtle alliteration of the letter M in these lines.

The “wild magnolia” begins a strong triple meaning, representing both the projects and his grandmother, Dorothy Flowers. and a widely respected New Orleans Indian Tribe.  “Mardi Gras Indians–the parade most white people don’t see. line: [Verse 4: Kanye West]
vault_lines: Look at my life, man, that's lessons on lessons on lessons
meaning:
Editor’s Note: This verse, which appeared on the music video, was omitted from the album version.

The verses of “Blessings” are unique metrically, in that they feature a regular use of trisyllables (stress patterns involving three, rather that two syllables – see the annotations on Verse 1 for a solid breakdown).

Kanye’s verse, interestingly, is in some ways the most unique; nearly all his lines end on a spondee (two stressed syllables in a row), balanced by a regular use of anapests (short, short, long) and tribrachs earlier in the line (tribrachs are three unstressed syllables in a row – this is cool because you almost NEVER see them). This makes total sense for Kanye – he loves to hit the rhyme hard, and drag it out:

They WANT me by the ROAD holding up CARDBOARD
so i GO extra HARD on the HARD FLOOR
right NOW I’m calling YOU from my HOME GYM
right after THAT nigga I’m GON' SWIM

The first two lines in the selection above are particularly ingenious. The internal (slant) rhyme on “road” and “hold,” the heavy “D” sounds, and the way the stresses fall repeatedly on the word “hard” gives the lines an incredible heaviness, underscoring the “hardness” of the both the lifestyle – and the floor – in question.

line: [Verse 1: Big Sean]
vault_lines: Look at my life, man, that's lessons on lessons on lessons
meaning:
This and the other verses are unique in that several lines fade in and out of trisyllabic meter– the syllables are pronounced in patterns of three rather than the patterns of two that are standard in rap.

Some lines are dactyllic (long, short, short), others are anapestic (short, short, long), and still others are amphibrachic (short, long, short). Another well known example of trisyllabic meter in rap is the “The Way I Am” by Eminem.

Usually the verses of “Blessings” begin dactylically, and then shift into variable trisyllabic hybrids, many of which are individually characteristic of each rapper. Here, Big Sean stays mostly dactylic, but has a fairly unique tendency to shift into pretty clean amphibrachs mid-verse.

Here are some examples from the opening rhymes (note the emphases are marked according to his performance, not necessarily how they would read on paper):

I lead a LIFE i deSERVE.
FUCK a vaCAY I feel BETter at WORK

This scheme is dactylic, with an extra stressed syllable on the rhyme.

BLEssings on BLEssings on BLEssings
LOOK at my LIFE man thats LESsons on LESsons on LESsons

This scheme is dactylic.

The DRINKS are the COLDest, the FUTURE the BRIGHTest
The FEAT not diVIded, the LOVE is diVIded

This scheme is amphibrachic.

meaning:
Big Sean employs wordplay in a scheme about ships. Sean refers to his chain (which he gestures at in the video) as half a “ticket”, which can be slang for a large amount of money. At the same time, when your ticket is halved (or ripped), it signifies that you have “boarded” the ship (or other mode of transport).

Continuing the theme of discrimination against people of color, Big Sean references the “ship,” which was how [African] slaves would be transported between places in a “slave ship.” Slavery was a huge problem in the U.S., African-Americans and men in Africa would be captured and become slaves, working in terribly cruel conditions.

The schooner Clotilda, found in Alabama, is said to be the last known slave ship. Although a sign of change for the better, Sean is not ignorant, and still sees how people of color are still oppressed and may be forced to live with fear nowadays.

line: But how I’m supposed to after the Tuskegee experiment? Where they took four hundred blacks, snuffed ’em syphilis Knowing that they might die never see or hear again
vault_lines: But how I'm supposed to after the Tuskegee experiment?
meaning:
The Tuskegee experiment was a study performed by members of the Tuskegee University in Alabama, beginning in 1932. 600 African-Americans were invited to be experimented on, with the promise of free health-care. The aim of the experiment was to observe the effects of syphilis, an STD which at the time, had no cure.

The experiment lasted 40 years, seeing African-Americans infected with syphilis monitored. No care was given to the men in order to effectively track the disease, therefore, the men suffered sight and hearing loss, or died a terrible death. Disease investigator Peter Buxton caught word of the experiment, and leaked it to the press, after his superiors chose to ignore his concerns.

Once shared in the media, public outrage ensued, until finally the experiment was shut down. Over a hundred men died, as well as the disease being passed on to relatives.
